summary: Describes how a backbone network running IPv6 inside can carry IPv4 multicast traffic between client networks. It focuses on the IPv4-over-IPv6 case, since the reverse has little real-world demand. It is part of the softwire work for transitioning from IPv4 to IPv6.

eli5.summary: Picture a road built only for one kind of vehicle that must carry another kind in sealed containers. This explains how to ship group video-style traffic of one type across a network of another type.

questions: how does ipv4 multicast work over ipv6
subtitle: How a backbone running IPv6 can carry IPv4 multicast between IPv4 client networks.

tldr.problem: During the move to IPv6, a backbone that runs only IPv6 inside may need to carry multicast traffic between client networks that still run IPv4.
tldr.mechanism: Border routers called AFBRs translate IPv4 PIM messages and group and source addresses into IPv6 ones using a one-to-one algorithmic mapping, then encapsulate the data across an IPv6 multicast tree.
tldr.outcome: IPv4 sources and receivers in different client networks can reach each other through the IPv6 core. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement.

facts.label: Scenario
facts.value: IPv4 clients over an IPv6 core

today: RFC 8638 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2019, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its mapping builds on RFC 8114.

sections.title: The Transition Problem
sections.content:
A backbone network may run one IP address family internally (the I-IP family) while connecting client networks that run another (the E-IP family). The backbone then has to offer both unicast and multicast transit to those clients. This RFC covers multicast and focuses on IPv4 clients over an IPv6 core, citing a lack of real-world use cases for the reverse case.

The idea is to use the multicast support already in the I-IP backbone to forward client E-IP multicast packets inside an I-IP core tree. That tree is rooted at one or more ingress Address Family Border Routers (AFBRs) and branches out to egress AFBRs. The RFC contrasts this with a multicast VPN approach, which maps many client trees onto fewer core trees but can waste bandwidth by delivering packets to AFBRs that have no receivers. It says the need for such aggregation does not exist for Internet-style multicast and has not been identified so far.
sections.eli5: A big highway that only understands one kind of address has to carry group messages for towns that use another kind. This is the plan for doing that.

sections.title: Terminology and Scope
sections.content:
An AFBR interconnects networks using different IP address families. For this purpose it runs both E-IP and I-IP control planes and encapsulates and decapsulates client packets for the core. An upstream AFBR is closer to the multicast source and a downstream AFBR is closer to a receiver. In this document the I-IP is IPv6 and the E-IP is IPv4.

Two prefixes are provisioned: uPrefix64, a /96 unicast IPv6 prefix for IPv4-embedded addresses, and mPrefix64, the /96 multicast equivalent. Because the IPv6 group address space is much larger, a client IPv4 tree can be mapped to a specific core tree, so an AFBR can map IPv4 group and source addresses to IPv6 and back algorithmically.
sections.eli5: The border routers are like customs offices at each end of a bridge. One end packs the goods, the other end unpacks them.

sections.title: The Mesh Multicast Mechanism
sections.content:
When a downstream AFBR gets an IPv4 PIM Join/Prune message for an (S,G) or (*,G) tree, it translates it into a PIMv6 message directed at the IPv6 address of the upstream AFBR. The upstream AFBR translates it back. The result is an IPv4 tree in the client networks and a matching tree in the IPv6 core.

The group address is mapped by prepending the provisioned mPrefix64 to the IPv4 group address, following the algorithm in RFC 8114. For sources, the RFC treats the core as source-specific multicast (SSM) only, to keep things simple. For an SSM client, the source S' is a virtual IPv6 address that leads to the upstream AFBR. For an ASM client, the (*,G) and (S,G) entries differ only in the WildCard and RPT bits, so the AFBRs clear or set those bits.

Every AFBR MUST announce the address of one of its IPv4 interfaces in the v4 field alongside its uPrefix64, over Multiprotocol BGP, and each announced uPrefix64 MUST be unique. That is how a translated message finds the right upstream AFBR.
sections.eli5: A request to join a group is rewritten into the other language, sent across, and rewritten back. The reverse address book is built into the addresses themselves.

sections.title: Control-Plane Details
sections.content:
State maintenance for IPv4 (*,G) and (S,G) follows the multicast AFTR behaviour in RFC 8114. An AFBR receiving an I-IP (S',G') message MUST check S'. If it starts with the unique prefix, the message is a translated IPv4 message and is translated back, so other PIM-SSM in the core is not affected.

A problem arises on switching from the shared tree to the shortest path tree. Core routers do not process (S,G,rpt) messages because the core is SSM only, so a downstream AFBR cannot prune a source from the shared tree and would get two copies of the data. The fix is for the downstream AFBR to encapsulate the (S,G,rpt) message (the RFC says it SHOULD) and unicast it to the upstream AFBR, where an interface agent collects them. It prunes the source only when every downstream AFBR has pruned it. The cost is some duplicated data while at least one downstream AFBR has not yet pruned. The agent is not needed in some deployments, such as when there is a single downstream router.

To keep duplication short, every AFBR is recommended to use the "switch on first packet" policy for SPT switchover. Register, Register-Stop, Hello and Assert messages are not translated and are out of scope.
sections.eli5: If one friend says "stop sending me that" but others still want it, the sender keeps sending until everyone has said stop.

sections.title: Data Plane and Packet Format
sections.content:
If at least one outgoing interface uses a different address family from the incoming one, the AFBR MUST encapsulate the packet using addresses derived from mPrefix64 and uPrefix64 to form an IPv6 multicast packet. On encapsulation the outer TTL and hop count SHOULD be set by policy. On decapsulation the inner values MUST NOT be incremented and MAY be decremented.

Encapsulation enlarges packets, so AFBRs MUST support fragmentation after encapsulation and reassembly. Path MTU Discovery SHOULD be enabled and ICMPv6 packets MUST NOT be filtered in the core. The RFC does not choose one encapsulation. It must accommodate the mechanisms in RFC 4925, and all AFBRs on the same core MUST implement the same one.

PIM packet formats stay as in RFC 7761, except that group and source addresses MUST be translated when crossing an AFBR. The RFC shows the Register-Stop message in IPv4 and IPv6 forms as an example.
sections.eli5: The goods go into a bigger box for the trip. If the box does not fit through a narrow tunnel, it can be split up and put back together.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The concerns in RFC 4925 and RFC 7761 apply. Extra work such as running interface agents could be exploited for a DDoS attack. An attacker might also set up many multicast trees in the edge networks and create too much multicast state in the core.

As defence, BGP policies SHOULD be carefully configured, for example so AFBRs accept Well-Known prefix advertisements only from trusted peers. The RFC also says cryptographic authentication of BGP sessions could be used. There are no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: A troublemaker could ask for lots of deliveries to overload the post office. So the post office should only listen to trusted partners.
